elections.note: Marred by abuse of state resources
elections.notes: Shares include votes against all candidates; invalid ballots are excluded. Kuchma, Marchuk and Kostenko ran as independents; Udovenko was the joint candidate of Rukh and Reforms and Order (filed under Rukh). The lead says Kuchma used state resources against his opponents and the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe called the conduct of the election "a disgrace". Turnout is the deciding round's, from the table (first round 70.15%, run-off 74.87%). First-round Others: 6 candidates (Vasyl Onopenko, Oleksandr Rzhavskyy, Yuriy Karmazin, Vitaliy Kononov, Oleksandr Bazyliuk, Mykola Haber). Region winners are the leading candidate in each region in the run-off, from the article's results-by-region table.

elections.note: Run-off annulled for falsification; re-run held

source.name: Wikipedia, citing the Central Election Commission

elections.notes: The Central Election Commission declared Yanukovych the winner of the 21 November run-off, but the Supreme Court annulled that round for widespread falsification (the lead's words) and ordered the repeat run-off of 26 December, which Yushchenko won; the annulled round flags no winner. Shares include votes against all candidates; invalid ballots are excluded. Yushchenko ran as an independent. Turnout is the deciding round's, from the table (first round 74.54%, run-off (annulled) 81.12%, repeat run-off 77.28%). First-round Others: 19 candidates. The article has no results-by-region table, so no region winners.

source.name: Wikipedia, citing the Central Election Commission

elections.notes: Snap election, decided in one round. The lead says it was not held everywhere: there was no voting in Crimea or Sevastopol (annexed by Russia) nor in much of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts; those two oblasts count as having voted because parts of them did. Poroshenko and Tihipko ran as independents, backed by UDAR and Strong Ukraine respectively, as the table notes. There was no "against all" option. Turnout is the table's (59.88%). Others: 11 candidates. Region winners are the leading candidate in each region, from the article's results-by-region table.

elections.note: Supreme Soviet of the Ukrainian SSR
elections.notes: The article has no results table. Its text says 442 of the 450 seats were filled in two rounds (4 March and 10–18 March), with the Communists winning 331 and the Democratic Bloc 111, and that eight seats stayed vacant because of low turnout (further rounds in six of them were set for 22 April). Deputies were elected in single-member constituencies, so there are no party votes. Turnout is the infobox's first-round figure (85%; 79% in the second round). The infobox shows the Communists down 119 seats, but there is no change column, so changes are null.

candidates.name: Party of Democratic Revival of Ukraine

elections.notes: Every seat was elected in single-member constituencies, with no party list, so votes are null (the table's figures are the constituency votes of each party's candidates). Seats are the 338 decided in the first two rounds, as the article's lead says; the other 112 were still vacant, and some districts stayed unrepresented for the whole term. Repeat elections are not included. Independents won the most seats, so they are flagged; the largest party was the Communist Party. The article has no party-list results by region, so no region winners. Turnout is the table's.

The table lists 5 seats as vacant. Electoral blocs are listed under their own names, as in the table: National Front (KUN–UKRP–URP); Forward Ukraine! (KDS–UKDP); Razom (LPU–PP); Bloc of Democratic Parties – NEP (DPU–PEV); SLON – Social Liberal Association (Viche–MBR); Fewer Words (SNPU–DSU). The table links "Party of Regional Revival of Ukraine" to the Party of Regions and "Agrarian Party of Ukraine" to the People's Party, so they share those keys. The article has no party-list results by region, so no region winners. Turnout is the table's, for the list vote.

elections.notes: Votes and shares are the party-list vote; seats are each party's total, 225 list plus 225 constituency seats. Independents won constituency seats only, so they have no list votes. Invalid ballots are excluded from the shares. Changes are the table's; "New" is shown as no change. The 27 vacant seats are constituencies in occupied areas where, the infobox says, the election could not take place (Crimea, Sevastopol and parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts). The Petro Poroshenko Bloc is today's European Solidarity (same article). The lead says voting did not take place in Crimea, Sevastopol or large parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts; those two oblasts count as having voted because parts of them did. Region winners are the party with the most list votes in each region, from the article's by-region table. Turnout is the table's, for the list vote.
